title: Documents close: the Church writes letters
hookLine: the Church still writes to the world, as Paul wrote to churches
tomorrow: a king says, you fed me. when did they ever see him hungry?

cards: Group projects have a typist. One person at the keyboard, everyone else talking over their shoulder. Near the end of Paul's letter to the Romans, the typist speaks up.
In the Douay-Rheims: "I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord." Paul talked, Tertius wrote, and the letter went off to people with names in a city far away.
This whole block has read the Church's documents. At the close, a question worth arguing: who are those documents actually for?

teach.b: There are two honest answers, and both have a case. One side says: leave them to people trained to read them. They come in different weights: a council's constitution, a pope's encyclical, an exhortation.
Read one paragraph alone and it's easy to make it say what you wanted. The Church gives bishops, priests and teachers to read them with you, and that's a gift, not a gate.
The other side says: they're letters, so open them.
Paul tells the Colossians that once his letter has been read among them, they should have it read in the church at Laodicea too. Read aloud, passed on.
And Laudato Si' says outright it's written to every person on the planet. Hear this block with both voices in mind. Numbered paragraphs, so a whole Church can land on the same line.
The Council: God speaking to us as friends, the joys and hopes of the world taken as the Church's own, no coercion in faith, one human family.

Then the popes: witnesses first, the person as the way, put out into the deep, an encounter, hope that changes life, a Church bruised from the street, time greater than space, everything connected, the woman at the market, Christ alive, he loved us.
One shape. Each was written to someone, and a letter isn't finished when it's sealed. It waits for an answer.

how: Church documents are read in parishes, schools and study groups, often a few numbered paragraphs at a time, and quoted in homilies so whole communities hear the same lines.

a rule that only experts may read official texts
the end of a block read as letters still being written

games.q: two views and a scribe — tap the pairs.
p: where Paul's letter was to be read next

s: Paul wrote every word of his letters with his own hand
in Romans, Tertius says he wrote the letter down.
Paul asked for one of his letters to be passed to another church
he tells the Colossians to have it read at Laodicea too.
every Church document carries exactly the same weight
a council's constitution, an encyclical and an exhortation differ in weight.

games.q: your friend posts a single line from an encyclical to win an argument online. you think documents should be read in context, with a teacher. what's the strongest case for her side, that anyone can read them?
o: they're letters: Paul had his read aloud and passed on, and some popes write to everyone.
a single line is all anyone needs; context is overrated.
the Church doesn't mind how documents get used.
games.why: both views are real. the letters were meant to be read and passed on, as at Laodicea; the Church also gives teachers so a paragraph isn't torn from its weight and context.

practice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper. Choose one person you'd write to about what you hold most dear: a child, a friend, your younger self. Write only the first sentence, by hand, and let it sit there unfinished.

wordCard.voice: Documents close. The end of this block of Church documents, read as letters: written to someone, passed on, waiting for an answer.

orig.note: Greek for a letter, the word Paul uses when he asks for his letter to be read at Laodicea.

carryVoice: Your line: still writing. The documents end here, and tomorrow the works of mercy begin. That's the block.
